concepts.title: Roster and Set-Builder Representation
concepts.definition: A set collects distinct objects picked out by a rule precise enough to settle membership for every candidate; it can be written by listing the objects in braces or by stating the common property of its members.
concepts.formula: A = {x : x satisfies the property p}
concepts.key_idea: Listing repeats nothing and ignores order; the builder form names one property instead.

solution_steps.explain: order and repetition do not change the set

solution_steps.action: for builder form state the characterising property after the colon
solution_steps.explain: the property must generate exactly the listed objects

concepts.title: Types of Sets and Cardinal Number
concepts.definition: Sets split by how much they hold: a void set has nothing, a singleton has exactly one object, a finite set has a countable stock of elements, and an infinite set cannot be exhausted by counting; the count for a finite set is its cardinal number.
concepts.key_idea: Integers strictly between endpoints a and b number one less than the gap between them.
concepts.textbook_ref: am11_003_sets.txt, section 3.3 singleton, empty, finite and infinite sets

solution_steps.action: take the gap between the two bounds
solution_steps.explain: the bounds exclude themselves when the inequality is strict

solution_steps.action: drop one for the strict bounds
solution_steps.explain: neither endpoint may be counted

concepts.title: Subsets and Counting Subsets
concepts.definition: A is a subset of B when every member of A also sits in B; a set with n elements has one subset for every way of choosing which elements to keep.
concepts.key_idea: Each element offers a keep-or-drop choice, so subsets double per element; dropping the set itself gives the proper count.
concepts.textbook_ref: am11_003_sets.txt, sections 3.4-3.5, subsets of {1,2,3} and n(P(A)) = 2^n

solution_steps.action: raise two to the element count
solution_steps.explain: every subset corresponds to one keep-or-drop choice per element

solution_steps.action: subtract the full set for the proper count
solution_steps.explain: a proper subset must miss at least one element

concepts.title: Power Set and Iterated Power Set
concepts.definition: The power set of A bundles all subsets of A into a single set; taking the power set of that collection again squares the element count once more.
concepts.key_idea: Each application of the power set doubles the element count, so P(P(A)) holds 2 raised to 2^n members.

concepts.title: Intervals on the Real Line and Their Length
concepts.definition: An interval is a stretch of the real line between two endpoints, keeping or dropping the ends as the brackets show; its length is the distance between the endpoints whatever the bracket style.
concepts.key_idea: Square brackets keep an endpoint, round brackets drop it; the length ignores the choice.

solution_steps.explain: both endpoints count when included

concepts.title: Union, Intersection, Difference and Complement
concepts.definition: Set operations build new sets: union gathers members of either set, intersection keeps only shared members, difference keeps the first set's members absent from the second, and complement keeps universal members outside the given set; complement turns unions into intersections under De Morgan.
concepts.key_idea: Union adds, overlap cancels, difference is one-sided, and complement reads the outside of the circle.
concepts.textbook_ref: am11_003_sets.txt, section 3.10 operations table, De Morgan laws, A - B examples

solution_steps.action: union: list every element of either set once
solution_steps.explain: members common to both appear a single time

solution_steps.action: intersection: keep only elements present in both
solution_steps.explain: no shared elements means the sets are disjoint

solution_steps.action: difference: strike from A anything that also sits in B
solution_steps.explain: A - B and B - A need not match

solution_steps.action: complement: keep universal elements missing from A
solution_steps.explain: De Morgan swaps union with intersection under the prime

concepts.title: Two-Set Counting and the Union Formula
concepts.definition: For finite sets, the union count is the sum of the separate counts with the shared region added back once; rearranging the same identity recovers the overlap, the only-one regions, the outside region, or the universal size.
concepts.key_idea: Disjoint sets skip the subtraction; every other region follows by adding or subtracting the overlap.

solution_steps.explain: the shared region is counted twice otherwise

solution_steps.action: remove the overlap from one side count
solution_steps.explain: leaves the members belonging to that set alone

solution_steps.explain: whoever lies in neither set

concepts.title: Least Possible Overlap of Two Sets
concepts.definition: When two sets sit inside a fixed population, their overlap cannot drop below the amount by which the separate counts together overrun the population; that least value equals the sum of the counts minus the population size.
concepts.key_idea: Pigeonhole pressure: counts that overflow the container force a shared region of at least the overflow.

solution_steps.action: add the two membership counts
solution_steps.explain: counts memberships before merging anyone

solution_steps.action: subtract the population size
solution_steps.explain: the overrun must sit in the shared region

concepts.title: Three-Set Venn Region Counting
concepts.definition: Counting over three sets needs pair overlaps subtracted and the triple region added back; the exactly-one regions emerge after stripping the double and triple overlaps off each single count.
concepts.formula: n_union3 = n_a + n_b + n_c - n_ab - n_ac - n_bc + n_abc
concepts.key_idea: Add singles, subtract pairs to undo double counting, restore the triple once.
